title: Instrumentation and control
where: the Electrical shelf's Power and machines at sea folder
folderRuns: Motors, Generators, Instrumentation and control, Subsea cable testing
blurb: How a plant measures itself and keeps itself in line: sensors and the 4-20 mA loop, control loops and PID, PLC logic, alarms and fail-safe trips.
from: any Brilliant course still reachable on brilliant.org that covers sensors, feedback or control (none is expected), and failing that the public benchmark of a Level 3 instrumentation and control unit (Pearson BTEC National Engineering and HNC units on instrumentation, control systems and PLCs)
others: the Pearson BTEC Level 3 National and HNC/HND Engineering unit specifications on instrumentation, control and programmable logic controllers, instrument makers' public application notes and handbooks (Fluke, Omega, WIKA, Endress+Hauser, Emerson/Rosemount, Yokogawa, ABB), public PLC documentation (Siemens, Allen-Bradley/Rockwell, IEC 61131-3 as a titled description), Control Engineering and ISA public articles, OpenStax and LibreTexts for the physics of sensors, HSE public guidance on alarm and safety systems (HSG and EEMUA 191 as titled descriptions only), and IEC 60751 and IEC 60584 for the PT100 and thermocouple tables as titled public values
syllabi: What a marine or naval engineering technician on the electrical path actually uses of this topic: the public apprenticeship standards on the Institute for Apprenticeships site for a Marine engineer, Naval engineering technician (or nearest), Engineering technician (electrical or control and instrumentation) and Maintenance and operations engineering technician; the STCW Code Table A-III/6 (electro-technical officer) and A-III/1 competence lines on control systems and automation; and the Pearson BTEC Level 3 and HNC unit lines on instrumentation, control and PLCs. Exact lines. Dan has no syllabi for his Navy courses ahead: plan against these and say where a choice is a guess
scope: Dan asked (3 Nov) for whatever is most relevant to his whole path, not only January: a Level 3 marine engineering qualification (general engineering first, then submarine and nuclear propulsion, which this course must never teach), leading rate engineering qualifications, and electrical work at sea. Instrumentation and control is the largest unbuilt foundation on that path: every plant system he will meet is measured, controlled, alarmed and tripped by it. About eight lessons in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) The measurement chain: sensor, transducer, transmitter, signal, display and controller; range, span, accuracy, resolution, repeatability and error; why calibration and zero and span checks. (2) Temperature: the PT100 resistance thermometer (about 0.385 ohm per degree, two, three and four-wire connection and why), thermocouples (the junction, extension cable, cold-junction compensation), thermistors and switches. (3) Pressure, level and flow: Bourdon tubes and strain-gauge and capacitive transducers, gauge, absolute and differential pressure; level from pressure (p = rho g h) and by float, capacitance or radar; flow from differential pressure (the square-root law) and by magnetic or turbine meters, in outline. (4) The 4-20 mA loop: why current, live zero and broken-wire detection, scaling a reading to a signal and back, loop power and the 250 ohm resistor, two-wire transmitters, checking a loop with a meter; 0-10 V in one line, HART in one line. (5) Control loops: open and closed loop, setpoint, measured value, error and output, on/off control with hysteresis (a thermostat or level switch), first-order lag and dead time, a feedback picture of the governor and AVR he already knows. (6) PID: proportional action and its offset, integral removing offset and its wind-up, derivative damping, overshoot and settling, tuning by feel with a live loop to tune, never a recipe that claims how any plant is tuned. (7) Logic and PLCs: relay logic to ladder logic, inputs, outputs and the scan, latches (start and stop circuits he knows from motor starters), timers and counters, interlocks and permissives. (8) Alarms, trips and fail-safe design: alarm versus trip, normally energised (de-energise to trip) circuits, high and low limits, deadband, voting (one out of two, two out of three) and why, first-up indication, bypasses and their danger. Each lesson opens with a puzzle he can feel his way through, then the rule, then typed-answer puzzles he works on paper. Examples from generic marine and industrial plant (a cooling water temperature loop, a tank level, a lube oil pressure trip, a compressor's start and stop, a 440 V generator's governor and AVR as loops); never claim how the Navy or a boat does it, and never touch reactor instrumentation or protection
